extracted.intended_audience: short fiction authors submitting to magazines; small-press and magazine editors
extracted.subtask_description: Practical editorial guidance for authors and editors of SFF short fiction covering submissions, selection, formats, distribution, business realities, and strategies to widen and diversify the submission pool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original submission length guideline (1000–4000 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the magazine's early days, all submissions were between 1000 and 4000 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This historical guideline influenced the types of stories submitted; editors and authors should be aware that explicit word limits shape the submission pool and the kinds of narratives sent in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word count and editing (trimming improves quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the maximum word count was increased (e.g., from 4000 to 8000), there was a noticeable drop in overall quality because authors were no longer forced to edit stories down; trimming can improve stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage authors to edit and trim; editors should consider how word limits incentivize stronger, tighter storytelling even as longer allowances permit greater scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow longer word counts when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Some stories cannot be told in 4000 words and expanding maximum limits has allowed the magazine to feature a broader range of stories and storytelling techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance inclusivity of longer narrative forms with vigilance about maintaining quality; recognize that some stories genuinely need greater length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage and publish international submissions and translations
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor actively cultivated increased international submissions (early years were >90% US; now ~55–60%), including publishing translated works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should outreach to global authors, publish translations to signal commitment, and expect that building an international pool may require deliberate effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial realities of translations (pay author and translator)
rubrics_metrics.description: With translations there is a financial obstacle: you have to pay an author and a translator; margins are tight and this influences selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magazines must budget for translation costs or limit translated content; transparent financial planning affects how many translations a publication can afford.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cast a wide net to find good stories
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor searches for good stories and believes casting the widest net possible is the right idea for finding quality work from diverse places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactively solicit, advertise widely, and be open to submissions from many regions and backgrounds to increase the chance of finding exceptional pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance for regional storytelling differences
rubrics_metrics.description: There are regional differences in storytelling techniques; editors with traditional expectations may have difficulty connecting with stories that deviate from their norm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop editorial tolerance and awareness for narrative conventions from different regions; recognize that deviation from a perceived center is not inherently poor work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide multiple formats to remove reading barriers (audio, print, online)
rubrics_metrics.description: To reach different readers, the magazine offers an audio edition for people who only have time to listen, a print edition for those who prefer print, and an online edition for those who cannot afford a subscription.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer formats that match audience habits and remove excuses that prevent reading; format diversity can grow readership and serve authors better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online free access as community growth strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping an online edition (even free) helps grow the reading community and serves authors, though it may reduce subscription income from readers who could pay but won’t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the trade-off between revenue and community-building; sometimes free access is strategically valuable for long-term field health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be flexible, adaptable, and willing to experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful magazines are willing to push at the edges, experiment, learn from mistakes, apologize when necessary, and adjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try new formats/features, evaluate results, and iterate; don't let confidence blind you to necessary changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency with readers and stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor is a fan of transparency and believes people appreciate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open about editorial decisions, policies, and business realities to build trust with staff, authors, translators, artists, and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operate with business discipline and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t forget this is a business; there’s responsibility to staff, authors, translators, artists, readers, and the field as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the magazine sustainably: manage finances, honor payments, and consider the broader impacts of editorial/business choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution is the primary problem (print and digital)
rubrics_metrics.description: The field’s biggest problem is distribution: print distributors have declined; digital subscription disruptions (e.g., Amazon cancellation) have been harmful; digital distribution into libraries is limited and often handled in suboptimal formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize developing reliable distribution channels (bookstores, libraries, direct subscriptions) and be aware of ecosystem fragility and vendor lock-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer reader-friendly digital formats (EPUB over PDF replicas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some library/distribution services build print-replica editions from PDFs rather than using EPUB, which readers of literary magazines typically prefer; conversion costs are an obstacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for and provide EPUB where possible; factor conversion costs and technical constraints into distribution planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convenience matters — remove technical/subscription hurdles
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial distribution systems sometimes resist serving a global audience and introduce technical hurdles that prevent readers from subscribing; convenience affects whether people subscribe and read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce friction in access (file formats, geographic availability, subscription flow) to improve reach and retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct subscriptions are important but limited by tools/resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasizing direct subscriptions is valuable, but tools and resources can limit what a magazine can do alone; collaboration with bookstores and libraries remains essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue direct-subscriber models while also investing in partnerships and infrastructure to extend reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use submission data to inform editorial outreach
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor used submission-system data to notice the low percentage of international submissions and then engaged in efforts to encourage more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track submission demographics and metrics to identify gaps and target outreach or policy changes strategically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission volume affects editorial strategy and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Submission volume has grown from <300/month to ~1250/month; changes in policy (like word-count increases) altered the submission pool and perceived quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor how policy changes influence both quantity and quality of submissions and adjust gates, guidelines, and editorial processes accordingly.
